skills.name: intersection_product_chow
skills.description: Compute the product of divisor classes in the Chow ring of a product of projective varieties using the known ring relations.
skills.preconditions: A product of projective varieties with explicit Chow rings and divisor classes to be multiplied is given.
skills.postconditions: The intersection class is expressed as a linear combination of basis classes in the Chow ring.
skills.example: In the product of a pair of projective lines, multiply the class of a vertical divisor with the class of a horizontal divisor to obtain the class of a point.

skills.name: generic_smoothness_application
skills.description: Apply the generic smoothness theorem to deduce that a morphism is smooth over a dense open subset of the target.
skills.preconditions: A morphism of finite type between varieties over an algebraically closed field is given, and the source is smooth.
skills.postconditions: There exists a dense open subset of the target over which the morphism is smooth, and the fibers have the expected dimension.
skills.example: For the projection from the incidence variety of points lying on a line to the space of lines, generic smoothness yields a smooth morphism over the open set of non‑vertical lines.

skills.name: finite_etale_check_via_jacobian
skills.description: Verify that a morphism is finite étale by checking finiteness and non‑vanishing of the Jacobian determinant on the relevant locus.
skills.preconditions: A morphism of varieties is known to be finite and the Jacobian matrix can be computed on an open set.
skills.postconditions: The morphism is concluded to be étale on that open set, implying it is unramified and flat there.
skills.example: For the map sending a point on a smooth curve to its image under an isomorphism, the Jacobian determinant is a nonzero constant, showing the map is finite étale away from the poles.

skills.name: lang_weil_point_estimate
skills.description: Use the Lang–Weil estimate to bound the number of rational points of a geometrically irreducible variety over a finite field in terms of its dimension and degree.
skills.preconditions: A geometrically irreducible variety defined over a finite field together with its dimension and degree is given.
skills.postconditions: An asymptotic formula is obtained showing the point count equals the field size raised to the dimension plus a lower‑order error term.
skills.example: For a smooth plane conic defined over a finite field, the estimate gives roughly the size of the field plus a bounded error.

skills.name: average_fiber_size_via_degree
skills.description: Relate the average cardinality of fibers over rational points to the geometric degree of a dominant morphism using the fact that the sum of fiber sizes equals the degree times the number of points in the target.
skills.preconditions: A dominant finite morphism between varieties over a finite field is given, and point counts on the target are known.
skills.postconditions: It is derived that the average fiber size approaches the degree as the field size grows.
skills.example: For the map from a finite cover of the projective line to the line itself, the average number of preimages of a rational point tends to the degree of the cover as the field size increases.

skills.name: parameter_space_of_hypersurfaces
skills.description: Construct the parameter space of degree‑d hypersurfaces in projective space as a projective space of global sections of the corresponding line bundle.
skills.preconditions: Projective space of a given dimension and an integer degree d are specified.
skills.postconditions: A projective space whose points correspond bijectively to hypersurfaces of that degree is obtained.
skills.example: The space of lines in the projective plane is realized as the projective space of linear forms, each point representing a line.

skills.name: tangency_condition_as_linear_subspace
skills.description: Translate a tangency condition between two hypersurfaces into a linear condition on the coefficients of one of them by imposing vanishing of the restriction of the differential along the other.
skills.preconditions: Two hypersurfaces are given, one fixed and smooth, and the other varies within a linear system.
skills.postconditions: The set of hypersurfaces tangent to the fixed one is identified with a linear subspace of the parameter space.
skills.example: For a fixed smooth curve of degree d in the plane, the condition that a variable line be tangent translates to the vanishing of the curve’s defining polynomial and its derivative at the point of contact, yielding a linear equation on the line’s coefficients.

skills.name: bezout_intersection_count
skills.description: Apply Bézout’s theorem to compute the number of intersection points of a collection of hypersurfaces in projective space when the intersection is proper and the hypersurfaces are in general position.
skills.preconditions: A set of hypersurfaces with known degrees intersect properly in projective space.
skills.postconditions: The total number of intersection points, counted with multiplicity, equals the product of the degrees.
skills.example: A hypersurface of degree d1 and another of degree d2 intersect in d1·d2 points (counted with multiplicity) when the intersection is proper.

skills.name: specialization_to_irreducible_components
skills.description: Use specialization from a generic fiber to a closed fiber to deduce the number of irreducible components of a family by upper semicontinuity of component count.
skills.preconditions: A flat family of varieties over a connected base is given, and the generic fiber is known to be irreducible.
skills.postconditions: It is concluded that every fiber has at most the same number of components, allowing inference of component count on specific fibers.
skills.example: In a family of plane curves obtained by varying a coefficient, if the generic curve is smooth (hence irreducible), then any specialized curve cannot acquire additional components.

skills.name: limit_of_normalized_point_counts
skills.description: Pass to the limit of normalized point counts over growing finite fields to extract a geometric invariant such as the average number of rational points per fiber.
skills.preconditions: For each finite field size, a count of rational points on a variety (or on fibers) is available, and the counts satisfy an asymptotic formula.
skills.postconditions: The limit of the ratio of the count to the size of the field (or to the point count of the base) exists and equals the desired invariant.
skills.example: For a family of elliptic curves parametrized by a line, the limit of the average number of points on the fibers divided by the field size approaches the trace of Frobenius averaged over the family.
